strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies two genuine limitations in existing dLLM RL (lack of verifiable rewards and unanalyzed probability estimation errors) with clear motivation and setup
Solid theoretical contribution: Section 3.3 rigorously analyzes how prediction confidence affects estimation error, providing formal bounds (Eqs. 10-11) with complete proofs
Strong empirical results on structured reasoning: Substantial improvements on Sudoku (+86.2%) and Countdown (+51.6%), with consistent gains over multiple competitive baselines

Comprehensive experimental validation: Well-designed ablation studies, sensitivity analysis for H and B, computational cost analysis, and training dynamics visualization demonstrating practical effectiveness
Clear presentation and effective communication: Figure 2 clearly illustrates the approach; paper is generally well-organized with compelling motivation for each component
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Tree-structured rollouts and self-distillation are known techniques; single-time forward pass estimation follows Diffu-GRPO directly. Main contribution is combining existing pieces (engineering-focused rather than methodological)

Theoretical analysis has significant gaps: (1) Confidence gap ϵ = max{ϵ_parent, ϵ_path} is pessimistic worst-case bound; (2) Theory does not directly justify or analyze the specific self-distillation loss design—only shows confidence helps, not why this particular schedule is optimal; (3) Bounds don't account for multi-step error propagation through tree

Self-distillation loss design lacks principled justification: Functional forms τ(t) = τ_max·(1-t/T)^β and λ(t) = λ_max·(e^{γt/T}-1)/(e^γ-1) appear ad-hoc; no systematic exploration of alternative schedules; hyperparameters appear task-dependent with limited guidance; why exponential for λ(t) but power-law for τ(t)?

Modest improvements on mathematical reasoning: GSM8K (+4.5%) and Math500 (+5.3%) show substantially smaller gains than puzzle tasks; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; no principled analysis of when/why method works best

Limited experimental scope and generalization: Only LLaDA-8B-Instruct tested; generalization to other dLLMs unclear; H=4 couldn't converge, so theoretical potential undemonstrated in practice; reimplemented baselines (†) raise fair comparison concerns; no multi-model or multi-scale evaluation

Block-wise adaptation constraint is inelegant workaround: Requirement that H divides number of blocks couples training and inference strategies; limits flexibility in decoding approaches; solution feels ad-hoc rather than fundamental

Missing analysis and clarity: No investigation of why method succeeds on puzzles but fails on math; actual variance reduction not quantified; insufficient discussion of failure modes; hyperparameter selection guidance lacking

strengths: Well-motivated identification of genuine challenges in dLLM RL: sparse/unverifiable rewards and unanalyzed log-probability approximation errors
Theoretical analysis relating prediction confidence to estimation error with formal bounds (Equations 10-11), providing principled justification for the self-distillation approach
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple reasoning tasks with substantial improvements on discrete problems (+86.2% Sudoku, +51.6% Countdown)
Thorough ablation studies validating design choices (Sections 4.4-4.5), particularly the comparison with reverse-scheduled self-distillation effectively demonstrating necessity of the time-schedule
Practical computational cost analysis (Table 3) demonstrating competitive training time compared to existing methods
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 2) and explicit algorithm description (Algorithm 1)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: tree-structured rollouts, hierarchical reward propagation, and self-distillation are standard RL techniques; application to dLLMs is incremental rather than conceptually new

Loose connection between theory and method: the error bound analysis confirms the intuitive result that high-confidence products approximate well, but does not rigorously justify the specific self-distillation design (Equations 12-15) or explain why advantage-weighted KL divergence is optimal

Experimental fairness concerns: multiple baselines are re-implementations (marked †) due to unavailable source code, raising questions about fair hyperparameter tuning; only LLaDA-8B tested, limiting generalizability across model scales

Task-dependent performance indicates potential overfitting to discrete problems with clean verifiable rewards: +86.2% on Sudoku vs. +4.5% on GSM8K, with no analysis of what distinguishes tasks where the method excels
Block-wise alignment constraint (Section 3.2) requiring H to divide L/b introduces an artifact fix rather than a principled design choice; practical impact not discussed

Fundamental scalability limitations: computational cost grows exponentially as B^H; H=4 experiments could not converge within practical constraints, limiting exploration of deeper reasoning hierarchies
Limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: τ_max, β, λ_max, and γ in scheduling all require justification; only H and B receive ablation study (Figure 3)

Self-distillation loss justification gaps: why minimize KL to advantage-weighted target rather than simpler entropy-based objectives? Why operate only on C_p^+ (positive advantages) when theory addresses all transitions?
Insufficient analysis of when and why the method works: no investigation of learned policy characteristics, sample trajectories, or fine-grained comparison of task properties affecting performance
Reproducibility concerns: code unavailability, numerous hyperparameter choices without justification, re-implemented baselines, and complex block-wise constraint implementation

strengths: Clear problem identification addressing two concrete limitations in dLLM RL (verifiable rewards and probability estimation)
Rigorous theoretical analysis with quantified bounds relating prediction confidence to estimation error (Equations 10-11), including complete proofs
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks with substantial improvements (+86.2% Sudoku, +51.6% Countdown, +4.5% GSM8K, +5.3% Math500)
Thorough ablation studies including reverse scheduling comparison and diversity-promoting loss baseline, effectively justifying design choices
Well-motivated framework design connecting theoretical analysis directly to the self-distillation loss component
Practical algorithm with full reproducibility details, clear Algorithm 1 description, and detailed hyperparameters
Extensive sensitivity analysis on tree parameters (H, B) and computational cost comparisons with baselines
weaknesses: Limited generalization scope: evaluated only on LLaDA-8B-Instruct; applicability to other dLLM architectures (Dream, SDAR) unclear

Theoretical contributions are incremental: core insight (confidence → lower error) is intuitive, bounds are loose, and proofs use standard techniques; simplified one-token-per-step assumption limits applicability

Computational efficiency concerns: requires ~2× training time of Diffu-GRPO; exponential growth with H and B forces practical use of small trees (H=2, B=4); could not train H=4 due to resource constraints

Self-distillation loss design lacks rigor: temperature schedule τ(t) and weight λ(t) appear arbitrary with minimal justification; no systematic hyperparameter sensitivity analysis across different scheduling functions

Questionable design choices: simple averaging for reward aggregation not justified as optimal; selecting only positive advantages for target distribution (C+_p) could bias learning; interaction between three loss components under-analyzed
Task-dependent performance: substantial variation across task types (discrete reasoning +86%, mathematical reasoning +4.5%) with limited analysis of when d-TreeRPO is preferable
Experimental gaps: no error bars or statistical significance testing; some baselines are reimplementations; zero-shot evaluation only; performance degrades on longer sequences (512-token settings)
Limited interpretability: no visualization of learned policies or tree structures; minimal analysis beyond theoretical motivation of why the method works empirically
Block-wise decoding dependency is architectural constraint that feels reactive rather than principled; comparability issue identified late and solution is somewhat ad-hoc

strengths: Clear problem identification: The paper identifies and articulates two genuine bottlenecks in dLLM RL (reward sparsity and probability estimation bias) that are well-motivated and practically important.

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 provides a rigorous high-probability bound showing estimation error decreases with model confidence, filling a gap in the dLLM literature. Proof is sound and well-presented in appendix.

Comprehensive technical approach: Addresses both identified problems coherently through tree-structured rollouts (reward granularity), theoretical analysis (probability estimation), and self-distillation loss (balanced exploration-exploitation).

Exceptional empirical results: Large improvements on puzzle tasks (+86.2% Sudoku, +51.6% Countdown) with consistent gains across two model sizes, multiple baselines, and different decoding strategies. Results on verification are reproducible.

Thorough experimental evaluation: Excellent ablation studies (Tables 3-4), sensitivity analysis across hyperparameters (Appendix E), budget-matched comparisons (Table 2), and direct measurement of probability estimation error improvement demonstrate rigor.

Strong evaluation methodology: Comparison with sparse-reward variants under identical computational budget convincingly isolates the value of fine-grained credit assignment. Probability estimation measured via Monte Carlo ground truth.

Clear presentation and visualization: Figure 2 effectively conveys the approach. Well-structured writing with good progression from motivation through method to experiments. Limitations honestly acknowledged.
weaknesses: Severely restricted applicability: Fundamentally requires automatically verifiable outcome rewards at leaf nodes. Evaluation limited to tasks with perfect verification (Sudoku, math correctness). Severely limits relevance to most NLP tasks (summarization, translation, open-ended generation quality). Authors acknowledge this but it's a critical limitation for ACL scope.

Theory-practice gap in Theorem 1: The bound depends on unobservable quantile q_{d,1-δ}. ϵ_{d,δ} defined circularly using both estimate and true value. No empirical validation of bound tightness. Theorem motivates 'increase confidence' but doesn't specify optimal level, leaving design choices (τ_max, β, λ_max, γ) empirical rather than principled.

Significant computational overhead: d-TreeRPO ~6.9× slower than Diffu-GRPO (598s vs 109s per batch), comparable to TraceRL/GDPO but much slower than efficient baselines. Exponential cost in H prevents using H>2 despite Figure 4a showing faster convergence. Cost-benefit not thoroughly justified.

Ad-hoc design constraints: Block-wise alignment requirement (H divides L/b) presented as necessary but feels like a patch. Limits flexibility in hyperparameter selection, unclear if general across architectures. Self-distillation schedule relies on four empirical hyperparameters without principled justification beyond Theorem 1 intuition.

Modest improvements on general reasoning: GSM8K +4.5%, Math500 +5.3% vs base (competitors already >80%). Puzzle tasks show massive gains but mathematical reasoning improvements are incremental, raising questions about cost-benefit of 6× computational overhead.

Limited direct impact of probability estimation improvements: Table 4 shows remaining error magnitude 1.25 ± 1.15 for d-TreeRPO still substantial. Error measurement uses only 32 Monte Carlo samples per token. Unclear if improvements come primarily from tree-structured credit assignment or probability estimation. No ablation separating these contributions.

Incomplete evaluation protocol: Only pass@1, zero-shot evaluation; no few-shot or pass@k analysis. Limits understanding of generalization and practical deployment. Limited to math/puzzle reasoning—no evaluation on other reasoning domains.

Block-wise decoding requirement not fully justified: Why this constraint is fundamental vs. implementation detail unclear. Impact on algorithm flexibility and applicability to other dLLM architectures not discussed.
Missing failure case analysis: Case studies (Appendix F) show only successes. No analysis of when/why d-TreeRPO might underperform. What task properties favor tree-structured RL? Unclear.

strengths: Clear problem identification with well-motivated challenges in dLLM RL: reward sparsity and probability estimation
Comprehensive empirical evaluation with 6 baselines, 4 tasks, 2 model sizes, and extensive ablations (tree parameters, self-distillation variants, hyperparameter sensitivity)
Strong empirical results on puzzle-based tasks (Sudoku +86.2%, Countdown +51.6%) with well-documented experiments and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
Concrete theoretical analysis (Theorem 1) providing a high-probability bound on estimation error, with complete proof
Effective ablation isolating fine-grained credit assignment benefits under identical rollout budgets (Table 2), demonstrating gains over sparse reward variants
weaknesses: Severely limited applicability: method requires verifiable outcome rewards at leaf nodes, restricting it to tasks with automatically checkable ground truth; inapplicable to most NLP tasks (summarization, translation, dialogue) that lack verifiable outcome rewards

Modest theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 establishes straightforward log-ratio bounds; connection to self-distillation design is loose and intuitive rather than rigorous; does not directly justify the specific advantage-weighted aggregation, time schedules, or KL objective

Incremental technical novelty: tree-structured RL is well-established; bottom-up value computation is standard Monte Carlo backup; self-distillation is known; the combination is relatively straightforward application to dLLMs

Marginal improvements on realistic tasks (GSM8K +4.5%, Math500 +5.3%) contrasting sharply with puzzle improvements (+51-86%); lack of analysis explaining performance disparities or when the method genuinely helps

Significant computational overhead and design constraints: requires B^H completions per query (16 with B=4, H=2); training 598s per batch versus Diffu-GRPO's 109s; block-wise alignment constraint (H must divide L/b) reduces decoding flexibility

Experimental limitations reducing generalization claims: Dream model excluded due to output format inconsistency (brittleness signal); evaluation limited to zero-shot pass@1; all four tasks have verifiable rewards (selection bias); single hyperparameter exception for different models suggests fragility

Weak connection between probability estimation approach and improvements: uses same single-forward-pass estimator as existing methods; self-distillation provides indirect fix for approximation bias rather than principled improvement to the estimator

Lacks analysis of when/why method succeeds: no explanation for 86% improvement on Sudoku versus 4.5% on GSM8K; no exploration of whether self-distillation benefits other dLLM RL methods; missing comparison of actual probability estimation quality

strengths: Well-motivated identification of genuine limitations in dLLM RL: reward sparsity and unanalyzed probability approximation errors

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 provides a rigorous, non-trivial high-probability bound relating single-pass estimates to path-wise probabilities, offering genuine insight into why prediction confidence improves estimation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model scales with substantial improvements (+86.2% Sudoku, +51.6% Countdown), comparing against 6 strong baselines

Rigorous ablation studies including crucial iso-budget comparisons (Table 2) isolating credit assignment benefits, sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters, and direct estimation error measurement (Table 4)
Elegant tree-structured solution for fine-grained credit assignment: natural bottom-up value propagation from verifiable outcome rewards to step-wise advantages
Thorough ablation of self-distillation loss with entropy/reward curves and reverse-schedule comparison providing strong empirical justification for design choices
Honest treatment of computational overhead with timing comparisons and acknowledgment of resource-performance trade-offs
Well-written paper with clear presentation, effective figures/tables, and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: framework only applicable to tasks with verifiable outcome rewards (exact-solution puzzles, math), fundamentally constraining applicability to open-ended generation and creative tasks

Indirect connection between theory and practice: Theorem 1 bounds log-ratio error w.r.t. path-wise probabilities but only indirectly justifies the single-pass estimate for unbiased expectation; the bound depends on unknown quantiles q_{d,1−δ}, and the self-distillation solution is a heuristic with limited connection to theoretical insights

Heuristic exploration-exploitation handling: time-scheduled self-distillation introduces many hyperparameters (τ_max, β, λ_max, γ) requiring careful per-task tuning; Appendix E shows non-trivial sensitivity, and exclusion of Dream model due to format inconsistency suggests experimental fragility

Insufficient computational analysis: method requires ~20 forward passes per gradient step; Figure 4a shows H=4 converges faster but is prohibitively expensive—this efficiency-performance trade-off deserves deeper investigation

Task-dependent performance: +4.5% on GSM8K and +5.3% on Math500 are modest compared to puzzle tasks (+86.2%), with insufficient analysis of why gains vary so dramatically or which task properties determine effectiveness
Block-wise adaptation constraint: requiring H to divide L/b adds inflexibility; limited discussion of alternative solutions or why this particular approach is necessary

Modest technical novelty: tree-structured rollouts, bottom-up value computation, and scheduled KL regularization are standard RL techniques; primary contribution is combining for dLLMs, which is somewhat incremental

Practical significance of probability error unclear: Table 4 shows log(p_true/p̂) differences of ~1.25 vs 1.32, but practical impact on policy optimization quality is unexplored; Monte Carlo estimation of p_true (32 samples) may have high variance
Narrow evaluation protocol: only zero-shot pass@1 scoring with no human evaluation, only reasoning tasks, limiting confidence in generality of improvements
Reproducibility concerns: many hyperparameters require careful tuning, Dream model excluded due to fragility, code availability not mentioned, suggesting potential challenges for practitioners
